text:
Andrew Lloyd Webber visits Korea as musical marks 40th anniversary this year British composer Andrew Lloyd Webber behind globally recognized musicals including "Phantom of the Opera" said Thursday that he is eager to explore Korea’s homegrown musicals during his stay and promised to return next year to watch more.
He is in Seoul this week to promote "Phantom of the Opera," which celebrates 40th anniversary of its premiere — it premiered in Korea 25 years ago.
The British composer acknowledged that the trip was overdue.
“I’ve been feeling a little bit ashamed of myself for not having come here earlier,” he said. “But this time I thought, I’ve got to come to Korea. I really must see what’s going on.”
About the active musical scene in Korea with many local productions making their own works, he said: “I think it’s fantastic to know that there is a musical theater culture coming from actually the country itself. I’m so thrilled that musical theater has become such a big part of life here.”
When it comes to the Korean cast of “Phantom of the Opera,” whose rehearsals he attended during the visit, Lloyd Webber praised the performers’ ability to act through the music and understand the lyrics. “Trust the music,” he said to the cast.
The Korean-language adaptation of the songs particularly impressed him, he said.
“The Korean language sat beautifully on the music,” the composer said. “It is stunning and I almost wished that I could hear it in Korean all the time.”
Also behind musicals “Cats,” “Jesus Christ Superstar” and “Evita,” Lloyd Webber has built a devoted following in Korea.
Since its Korean premiere, “Phantom of the Opera” has alone drawn more than 1.5 million theatergoers. The musical attracted more than 160 million people worldwide since its world premiere in 1986, according to its production.
While welcoming experiments in performing arts, he said there should be a distinction between human creativity and artificial intelligence (AI).
AI, he argued, has the ability to processes existing materials but can't generate genuinely original artistic ideas, like turning T.S. Eliot’s poems into “Cats,” or the theft of the Mona Lisa into a musical work, which he is currently working on.
His forthcoming musical will explore how the theft of the Mona Lisa helped turn the painting into a global icon. The subject will step out of her frame to speak her mind, he added.
The beauty of live performance, meanwhile, is that it offers audiences a unique, irreproducible experience each night, he said. Attracting younger audiences requires compelling subjects and welcoming atmosphere in the theater, not simply recycling familiar productions.
“Young people will go anywhere where they feel welcome and where there is a good story,” he said.
The anniversary production runs Dec. 22 through Feb. 2027, at Blue Square’s Woori Bank Hall in Seoul.
